strengths: The mean-point correspondence is a simple, original, and useful construction for practical four-point, three-view pose estimation. Reusing established five-point and P3P solvers avoids the complexity of dedicated polynomial solvers and makes the contribution accessible to geometric vision systems.

The empirical support is substantial: 90,000 camera triplets across 18 scenes from three datasets, evaluated within both PoseLib and GC-RANSAC. The supplement includes synthetic geometry and noise experiments, outlier experiments, threshold sensitivity, and an alternative metric covering all three camera pairs.

Table 2 demonstrates useful efficiency even against an enhanced five-point baseline. On PhotoTourism, 4p3v(M)+R+F+ENM achieves AUC@10 of 76.16 versus 76.20 for 5pt+P3P+R+F+ENM, while reducing runtime from 56.52 to 44.51 ms. On Cambridge, both achieve 66.31, with runtimes of 32.48 versus 47.07 ms. These results substantiate practical value independently of the comparison with homotopy continuation.

The component ablations explain how refinement, filtering, and early non-minimal refitting make approximate hypotheses useful. Parameters are selected on a separate validation scene, and the manuscript provides a code link. Its acknowledgement of approximation bias and weaker standalone performance is scientifically helpful. Overall, the supported practical contribution favors acceptance despite the reservations below.
weaknesses: The speed comparison with homotopy continuation has a consequential initialization confound. Section 8.3, footnote 8, reports approximately 45 ms of network/data loading per RANSAC invocation; Table 2 reports only 64.10 ms total for HC on PhotoTourism. Loading can be amortized across triplets, so these timings do not establish the claimed speed advantage for repeated use. Accuracy improvements remain supported, but initialization and steady-state computation need separate interpretation.

The strongest speed–accuracy claims exceed the comparisons shown. Figure 4 omits the +R+F versions of the five-point baseline, although Table 2 shows that these modifications improve it. Against 5pt+P3P+R+F+ENM, the most accurate proposed variant improves AUC@10 by only 0.94, 0.64, and 0.31 percentage points across the three datasets, while taking approximately 1.7–2 times longer under early termination. The results support useful operating points, rather than uniform superiority; matched-budget curves for the enhanced baseline are missing.

The theoretical support does not characterize when the approximation yields a reliable pose. Lemma 1 bounds surrogate epipolar error by the triangle's spatial extent, which can be large, and supplies no bound on pose error or refinement convergence. Figure 9 confirms nonzero errors even without measurement noise. The claim that ENM makes scene dependence negligible is therefore stronger than the demonstrated geometric understanding, although the extensive empirical results mitigate this limitation.

There is a correctable reporting concern in Table 6: all six Cambridge metrics are identical between the affine and mean-point +R+F variants, and again between their +R+F+ENM variants. These repeated rows warrant verification because they affect the supplementary comparison between solver families. This does not independently undermine the broader main-table evidence.
